items.title: Sub-second wait truncates to zero, so Retry-After tells the client to retry immediately
items.body:
## Summary

A wait shorter than one second truncates to zero, so a throttled client is told to retry immediately. With a quota whose replenish interval is under a second, every 429 carries `Wait for 0s` and `Retry-After: 0`.

## Where

`src/lib.rs:125-127`, and the same three lines again at `:293-295`:

```rust
let wait_time = negative
    .wait_time_from(DefaultClock::default().now())
    .as_secs();
```

`Duration::as_secs` truncates toward zero, so any wait under one second becomes `0`. The value is stored as `wait_time: u64` in `src/errors.rs:9` and reaches the client twice:

- the error message, `src/errors.rs:7` and `:50`: `Too Many Requests! Wait for {wait_time}s`
- the `Retry-After` header built from the same value

Both say zero for a genuine wait of, say, 200ms.

## Why it matters

`Retry-After: 0` reads as "retry now". A client that honours the header does exactly that, so under sustained load every throttled caller retries at once and none of them waits. That is the behaviour the limiter exists to prevent, and it appears precisely when the limiter is working.

It is not a rare configuration. Any quota that replenishes faster than once per second produces sub-second waits as the normal case, so those deployments never see a usable value.

The message is worth fixing alongside the header, since `Wait for 0s` gives an operator reading logs no way to tell a fast quota from a broken one.

## Suggested fix

Round up rather than truncate, so a non-zero wait is never reported as zero:

```rust
let wait_time = negative
    .wait_time_from(DefaultClock::default().now())
    .as_secs_f64()
    .ceil() as u64;
```

`.as_secs().max(1)` also works if you would rather not introduce a float, though it reports 1 for a 1.5 second wait where the ceiling reports 2.

RFC 9110 defines `Retry-After` as an integer number of seconds, so rounding up is the standards-compatible answer and one second is the smallest honest value the header can carry.

If sub-second precision is worth exposing, a separate accessor on `GovernorError::TooManyRequests` returning the raw `Duration` would let callers build their own header while the default stays correct.

## Workaround for anyone hitting this

Clamp the value in your own error handler before it reaches the response, and write the clamped number over both the message and the header, since the two are populated from the same field.

items.title: Make it possible to disable `quanta` feature of governor
items.body:
There is an issue in `governor` caused by using `quanta` clock by default. `quanta` uses TSC as clocks, and in case where TSC clocks are not synchronized between CPU cores, moving the thread to another CPU core may lead to randomly block the request: https://github.com/boinkor-net/governor/issues/299
Might be the reason for https://github.com/benwis/tower-governor/issues/55

I tried to replace line https://github.com/benwis/tower-governor/blob/bfe199cdf0a957446fe55ddb9d6e599b80461b10/Cargo.toml#L18 with
```
governor = { version = "0.10.0", default-features = false, features = ["std"] }
```
but compilation failed because code assumes that default clock is quanta and `QuantaInstant` is imported here:
https://github.com/benwis/tower-governor/blob/bfe199cdf0a957446fe55ddb9d6e599b80461b10/src/governor.rs#L6

I suggest making it possible to compile without `quanta`, and turn `quanta` into a feature of tower-governor. Maybe enable it by default for compatibility or disable and make a breaking release.

items.title: Is there a way to get the request body in the KeyExtractor?
items.body:
Protecting other routes was very easy thanks to this crate, however I am really struggling with protecting my login route by using the login parameter in addition to IP. This parameter is passed in the request body.

I cannot find a way to get the body of a `Request<T>`. The body ends up being of type `T`, and `trait KeyExtractor` enforces that signature. I believe trying to enforce stricter trait bounds in a function and calling that wouldn't work anyway, so this is likely a dead end.

This issue exceeds my rust abilities at this point, can you/someone perhaps give me a point in the right direction? Thanks!

items.title: Any plans to support jsonrpsee?
KeyExtractor generic parameter makes conditional runtime handling difficult
items.body:
In my app I'd like the user to have an option to rate-limit based on IP (if running in a standalone mode), or reverse proxy headers. However currently conditionally setting the extractor makes the types be incompatible.

Seems to me like either `GovernorConfig` should drop the `K` generic and `Box` key_extractor to `Box<dyn KeyExtractor>`, or at very least `impl KeyExtractor for Box<T> where T: KeyExtractor` (and maybe for `Arc<T>` too), to allow people to have unified `GovernorConfig<Box<dyn KeyExtractor>>` that can have runtime-conditional key extractor.
